opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Kim, thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group, and we don't work for any company, union or party. Nothing you tell me will be linked to your name, so feel free to tell me what you'd say out loud and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Okay, sure. I'm between clients, so I can talk now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's fine. I use it to make nail art ideas sometimes. Customers show me pictures from the AI and I copy them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing really changes for me. People still want their nails done. Those painting machines in the mall, they only do simple colours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same. Work six days, send money to my parents, save a little for my daughter. Maybe learn the new gel extensions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Normal.

S0.say: It's fine. Customers show me AI nail art pictures and I copy them.
S0.think: Nothing changes; people still want nails done and the mall machines only do simple colours.
S0.do: Works six days, sends money to her parents, saves for her daughter, and learns gel extensions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people will always want to be pampered. A machine can't massage your hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The kiosks get better slowly. Maybe in ten years they do the art too. But I'm good at detail work and my regulars ask for me. I think I'm okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get better at the hard designs, the hand-painted ones, so I'm worth more. Maybe post my work online to get new clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A small worry.

S1.say: People will always want to be pampered. A machine can't massage your hands.
S1.think: The kiosks may slowly learn art too, but her detail work and loyal regulars should keep her okay.
S1.do: Builds skill in hand-painted designs and posts her work online for new clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's hard for families. A lot of my customers work in offices. I'd listen to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When people lose jobs, nails are the first thing they stop. It's extra, not needed. I'd lose some clients. My husband and I have nothing saved, and my parents need money every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Offer cheaper basic service, keep everyone coming even if less often. Work more Sundays. Tell my parents we may send less for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Money is always tight already.

S2.say: It's hard for families. Many of my customers work in offices, and I'd listen to them.
S2.think: Nails are the first thing people cut when they lose work, and her family has no savings while her parents need monthly support.
S2.do: Offers a cheaper basic service, works more Sundays, and warns her parents she may send less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government should help families, not only the rich. But people should still work, that's important.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My customers losing good jobs is bad for me. Some rich ladies would come more, maybe. But in my area, most are normal people. I think I'd lose a third of my money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ask to move to a salon in a richer area. Do house calls for older ladies. Cut our spending, no eating out, no new things for my daughter except school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. I think about it at night.

S3.say: Government should help families, not only the rich. But people should still work.
S3.think: Her mostly ordinary clients would lose good jobs, maybe costing her a third of her income.
S3.do: Seeks a salon in a richer area, offers house calls to older women, and cuts family spending.
S3.feel: Worried, thinks about it at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say no robot should touch my hands. I'd tell customers that real people still do it better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: But I worry. If the robot arm can cook and build, the nail machine can paint gel and do art too. It would be cheap, and in the mall. Customers with no job would pick cheap. My whole family depends on my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn something more, maybe eyelashes or skin care, things that need a person. Talk to my husband about taking any extra work he can. Stop sending money to my parents for a while, which would hurt them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Lashes and skin care, do you think a machine couldn't do those too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Maybe. I hope it takes longer, because it's close to the face. People get nervous. That gives me some time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. For my daughter and my parents.

S4.say: No robot should touch my hands. Real people still do it better.
S4.think: If robot arms can cook and build, cheap mall machines can do gel and art too, and her whole family depends on her hands.
S4.do: Learns lash or skin care work, asks her husband to take extra work, and pauses money to her parents.
S4.feel: Scared, for her daughter and parents.
